title: The Same Window, Morning and Evening

# The Same Window, Morning and Evening

## Why a Repeated View Matters

Impermanence is easier to notice when something stays the same long enough to show how it changes. A window you pass every day can become that steady point. You are not trying to fix your mood or force insight. You are simply observing what is different after several hours have passed.

This practice fits everyday self-reflection because it takes seconds, requires no special equipment, and can be done inside an ordinary routine. It also works as a way to calm the mind: naming what you see occupies attention without analysis. You do not need to believe in any particular philosophy, and you do not need to set aside a formal meditation period.

The goal is not to produce beautiful observations or to prove that life is fleeting. The goal is to build a small habit of looking twice at the same thing. Over time, that repetition can make change feel less abstract and more immediate. It is a low-stakes way to meet impermanence without needing a retreat, a journal, or a teacher.

## The Practice: Morning and Evening at One Window

Follow these steps. You can complete the whole cycle in one day, and you can repeat it as often as you like.

1. Pick one window. Choose a window you can see in the morning and again in the evening. It does not need to look onto a garden or a street. A window onto a wall, a courtyard, or a parking lot works as long as you can see something outside it. If you share a home, choose a window you can reach without disrupting others.

2. Look in the morning. Stand or sit at the window soon after you wake. Notice one thing you see. It might be the color of the sky, the position of a shadow, a parked car, or a leaf on a branch. Name it silently or out loud. Do not judge whether the view is pleasant or interesting, and do not try to describe the whole scene.

3. Look again in the evening. Return to the same window before you go to bed or after dinner. Notice one thing you see now. It can be the same object as before, or something different. If it is dark outside, notice what is visible because of interior or exterior light.

4. Compare the two observations. Ask yourself: What changed? What stayed the same? You do not need a profound answer. A simple observation is enough. If nothing seems different, that is also a valid result.

5. Write one line. Keep a small notebook or a note on your phone. Record the date, the window, and one sentence about the difference you noticed. Example: "Morning: gray sky and empty bench. Evening: dark sky and a person sitting on the bench."

Repeat for as many days as useful. There is no required streak, and missing a day does not invalidate the practice.

If mornings are rushed, you can look at the window before leaving the house rather than immediately after waking. If evenings are irregular, choose a consistent anchor, such as after your last meal or before brushing your teeth. The exact clock time matters less than using the same window twice within one day.

## An Example from an Ordinary Tuesday

Here is how the practice might look for one reader.

Morning: At 7:15 a.m., Maya looked at the kitchen window. She saw a delivery truck parked at the curb and a single pigeon on the sill. She noted: "Truck and pigeon."

Evening: At 9:10 p.m., she returned to the same window. The truck was gone. The sill was empty. A streetlight had come on, casting a yellow rectangle on the pavement. She noted: "No truck, no pigeon. Light on the ground."

She did not draw conclusions about productivity, loss, or the passage of time. She only recorded that the view had changed. The next morning, the truck was back. That pattern itself became part of the reflection, reminding her that return and departure can happen within twenty-four hours.

You do not need to name a truck or a pigeon. Any visible detail counts.
